https://www.telegraph.co.uk/women/life/c.title: Charlotte Church: ‘People have an impression of who I was years ago – I want to claw back that narrative’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/women/life/c.subtitle: The singer talks modern parenting and her surprising new venture – and why she’s ready to risk her fortune on it
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/women/life/c.text:
Through the strange digital intimacy of Zoom, Charlotte Church is waving at me from the toy-strewn sitting room of her large home in Dinas Powys, south Wales. Charlotte – who first found fame as ‘Voice of an Angel’, an operatic child prodigy, before hitting the headlines as a ladette multimillionaire star – is sitting cross-legged on the floor.
Her one-year-old baby Freida is clamped to her breast while her two older children, Ruby, 14, and Dexter, 12, keep popping in and out looking for keys and schoolbooks. Three fluffy white dogs (Selma the spoodle, Holly the cavapoo and Nilson the goldendoodle) and a large nylon child’s play tunnel complete the picture.
Amid this scene of cosy domestic chaos is the 35-year-old singer, in an oversized yellow sweatshirt and entirely make-up free (‘I hardly ever bother with make-up these days,’ she says). Her face looms right into the camera: ‘God, look at the bags under my eyes,’ she says in her lilting Welsh accent. ‘You can tell I hardly ever do these Zoom things, can’t you?’
Today’s earth mother is a far cry from Charlotte’s wild-child image at the height of her fame in the early noughties. I first met her in 1999 when she was just 13, and her record company Sony asked me to do her media training – her debut album Voice of an Angel had been launched the previous year.
She was bright, talkative, and seemed to find the concept that she was suddenly world famous completely hilarious. Over the next eight years, whenever we would meet for interviews, she became increasingly opinionated about her image and musical direction, and was always open, smart as a whip and very entertaining.
She’d first found overnight fame in 1997, after singing Pie Jesu over the telephone on This Morning. Days later she was introducing her aunt Caroline, a wannabe singer on Jonathan Ross's Big Big Talent Show and she was immediately signed by Sony to record Voice of an Angel, which sold six million copies worldwide.
The working-class girl from Cardiff quickly became a child superstar, whisked around the world to appear on TV shows across the globe and to sing for presidents, the Pope and the Queen, accompanied by her mum Maria or stepfather James.
However it wasn’t long before she began to follow the well-worn trajectory from angelic child star to teen rebel. Rarely out of the tabloid press, she was pilloried for being a ‘chavvy ladette’, with endless photos of her falling out of nightclubs alongside her mates in Cardiff, her ‘rebellion against the whole celebrity thing’.
In 2006 she was given her own chat show by Channel 4, The Charlotte Church Show, which saw her crowned Best Female Comedy Newcomer at the British Comedy Awards. By the age of 25 she was worth an estimated £7 million.
But after living her tweens, teens and 20s under the harsh glare of the celebrity spotlight, Charlotte has chosen to spend the past decade living largely under the radar with her children and husband, fellow Welsh musician Jonathan Powell, and has changed her life entirely, ‘because I wanted to be a better member of society,’ she says.
After working as a performer from the age of 11, she decided to opt out, using her money to live the lifestyle she wanted, fund social projects (including her own school), supporting relatives and a more alternative music career. Although she won’t talk about her finances, she admits, ‘I was lucky to be able to afford that option.’
Now she is back with a reality TV series, Charlotte Church's Dream Build, documenting her ambitious plan to convert Rhydoldog, the 16th-century former home of Welsh designer Laura Ashley in Elan Valley, Powys, into an off-grid, eco healing retreat.
Having bought it in May this year for £1.5 million, the renovation costs are expected to total a further £1.2 million. The plan is for seven bedrooms, and a flexible pricing structure to make it accessible to as wide an audience as possible. The retreat will also have – at Charlotte’s instigation – a ‘history room’ dedicated to Laura Ashley.
‘I’m not frightened of another wild ride… My life has been a wild ride that I chose to come off,’ she says, deftly extricating Freida and settling her down next to her.
Charlotte wears: jacquard jacket, £450, Lisou; recycled-silver earrings, £255, Loveness Lee; necklace, £309, Oroton.
‘Being in the public eye at a young age was complicated and anxiety inducing. You get to a point where it just gets too much and that’s what happened to me 10 years ago. I wanted to be at home with my children, with Jonny. I wanted time out. It’s something I knew I needed to do and it’s been really good for all of us.
‘I have been offered so many TV shows and music projects over the years but always turned them down and just a year or so ago I felt in the right place to do something, say something.
‘People have an impression of who I was years ago and I want to claw back that narrative, and be who I am now. This wasn’t a decision taken lightly because it involves all my family, but I think I’m ready to take that risk, to be authentic and put myself back out there.’
Brought up in Llandaff, Cardiff, Charlotte is the only daughter of housewife Maria and Stephen Reed, a computer engineer. Stephen walked out on Charlotte and her mother when she was two, and in 1992 Maria married her second husband, James Church, who adopted Charlotte in 1999.
She remained estranged from Stephen up until his death from Covid earlier this year and has always referred to James as ‘Dad’. ‘Because that’s what he is, in every sense of the word,’ she says.
The documentary gives a very surprising, and endearing perspective on a smart, strong woman who has absolutely taken her own path away from fame. A long way from the shiny, perfect world of the Kardashians, you see Charlotte make-up free, knocking down walls, and digging out trenches.
And she lives out her eco values in her daily life, eating organic, local produce, recycling and educating herself and her children about the planet. ‘I do everything I can because the planet is pretty much the most important issue of our time,’ she says.
Ruby and Dexter – her two children from a five-year relationship with rugby player Gavin Henson, which ended in 2010 – are not allowed mobile phones. ‘Their dad lets them have phones in his house, but I won’t allow them. We waste our lives on screen time, social media is damaging to young minds, you’re wanting and buying stuff you don’t need. I’m not having it,’ she laughs.
Her two older children are home-schooled but spend 50 per cent of their learning time at the Awen Project, an outdoor educational facility partnered with the Woodland Trust. Set up by Charlotte and Jonny in 2019 with additional funding from other sources, including philanthropists, it offers supplementary learning to children aged nine to 14, school sessions are held in the woodland a mile from their home.
Charlotte wears: dress, £249, Coast; pearl necklace, £165, Missoma; diamond and sapphire cuff, £900, Hannah Martin; boots, £250, Dune London.
‘I always felt the traditional school system was too structured,’ she says. ‘I homeschooled my children for years but I knew they needed something more.’
The premise of the school, which has 15 pupils and is entirely funded by Charlotte, is to ‘give children a connection to the land, a sense of responsibility for themselves and others, and for them to learn about how we can have better societal values’. But it’s also to make children feel they are ‘listened to’. Several pupils came as elective mutes and within months were chairing the ‘daily democratic meetings’.
With Charlotte focusing on Rhydoldog, Jonny is now doing the lion’s share of the school teaching (twelve hours per week) and they regularly draft in guest speakers, experts and educators to talk to the children. She describes their job as ‘giving a bigger picture', so alongside traditional academic subjects, 'we do art projects, singing, performance.’
I remind her that when she was 16 she told me she’d got eight A-grade GCSEs (including three A*s) and then how, two years later, aged 18, after being criticised by the press for carousing with her schoolmates in pubs, clubs and bars she told me: ‘I haven’t been to uni but these are my uni years. I’m just doing what every kid my age does and I’m not apologising for it.’
‘God, I could be a real tool back then,’ she laughs, then adds: ‘But I was rebelling in my own way. I didn’t want to be in London. I never wanted to be friends with other celebrities; I wanted to be who I was. I can see why people thought I was common as muck, but part of me was having a ball and part of me was having a hard time.
‘I rebelled against that whole celebrity image. I would never diet but people would ask me in a roundabout way how I felt about “being bigger”. I also had family issues going on [her mother, who suffers from bipolar disorder, attempted suicide in 2005] and it was too much.’
In 2011 Charlotte gave testimony to the Leveson inquiry about her treatment by the press. ‘That was a massive learning curve,’ she says. ‘I’ve always been a feminist but I became more so, more educated. We needed to change the way society looks at women, at mental health. And yes, Britney has been part of that lesson. We have to take responsibility and change.’
The real jeopardy of Charlotte Church's Dream Build, though, is that Charlotte – who is totally hands-on with ‘everything from the size of the windows to the planting in the grounds’ – is risking all her remaining money on her dream to make Rhydoldog fully sustainable, powered by a hydro-mill and solar panels.
Inevitably, within a matter of months she was hugely over-budget. The off-grid batteries alone cost £300,000, wiping out her entire original ‘spend’ money. She planned to spend less than £150,000 doing up the barns and outhouses but was told that she would have to almost quadruple that budget. ‘I’m going to have to get a mortgage, then,’ she says, after further conversations with her builders.
I tell her that watching the documentary gave me anxiety. ‘This is all of your money, Charlotte!’ She laughs. ‘Well, for the majority of my life I have had the privilege of never having to worry about money,’ she says. ‘But for most people money is a survival dance. I’ve had other survival dances in my life but now money too is part of my survival dance.
‘I don’t want to be somebody sitting on piles of money, leaving millions of pounds or even thousands of pounds to my children. I want to build something that is bigger, means more and can sustain us and other people.’
I want to know why, in her fourth decade, after living a vivid, larger-than-life existence, this new direction means so much to her. There is a pause. ‘I lost my child,’ she says bluntly. ‘I love being a mother. From the first moment I was pregnant with Ruby I felt incredible. I loved pregnancy, I loved breastfeeding, I wanted more children.’
In 2017 she became pregnant with her first child by Jonny. They were both ecstatic. But sadly Charlotte suffered a miscarriage and went through what she describes as ‘the beautiful pain’ of giving birth to their child.
‘It was such a difficult time,’ she says. ‘You experience birth and death in one moment, which is so very hard, but it’s your child and there’s also something beautiful in that.’
Afterwards she was consumed by grief. Her way of dealing with her sadness was to externalise her emotions, and get closer to nature. ‘I just felt this pull,’ she says. ‘I went cold-water swimming three times a week and a month or so after we lost her, Jonny and I spent two weeks climbing the Dolomites. In the vastness of nature we cried, we laughed, and we felt that we were really healing, that everything in our life was put into perspective.’
It was on that trip she and Jonny decided to get married. ‘We always said we’d get married in our 50s if we’d weathered the storms of growing up together, but then both of us felt, why would we wait? The ceremony of the wedding just seemed very important.’
They married at a Cardiff register office a few months later, before having a ceremony in the garden of their home surrounded by 100 of their family and friends. Charlotte began thinking about a new direction. ‘I knew how much nature has changed my life and I wanted others to experience that.’
And she believes that music has the power to help heal trauma, so is now training to be a sound therapist, alongside her role as an educator and an activist. She has protested against Trump, marched for Black Lives Matter, is a member of Hacked Off – the campaign for a free and accountable press, whose board includes Hugh Grant – and she supports Welsh independence.
She is helped in the restoration by friends, local builders, her wonderfully wise stepdad James (her parents have contributed £300,000 to the costs). Charlotte admits that unless the project is finished by this summer, she will be broke. So far, nothing is on track. ‘Yes,’ she says. ‘“On track” isn’t something I can say.’
We talk about other things, other relationships. She and Gavin – who in 2019 married his long-term partner Katie Wilson Mould – have remained friends. He lives close to Charlotte’s home and shares care of their children.
She continues to perform, doing festival gigs with her musical collective the Late Night Pop Dungeon, covering songs by the likes of Bowie and Britney alongside her husband and fellow collective member, Jonny. ‘Music will never not be part of my life,’ she says.
Her bond with her dad is particularly moving in the documentary. In 2019 Charlotte announced that James, 55, had been diagnosed with AL amyloidosis – a disease similar to blood cancer – and told he had a year to live.
He phlegmatically accepts Charlotte’s initial plans to have no locks on doors, not to instal en-suites in the bedrooms, and to tear out the original stained-glass windows, saying: ‘When you go through big stuff like we all have, you can’t stress, you just go with the flow and see how it turns out.’
She smiles and tells me she’s now had to go back on every one of those decisions. ‘You have to compromise,’ she laughs. ‘I want to create something special because we live in this busy, anxious world. I want to be able to help make change. And if I really run out of money, you’ll see me on all those celebrity shows because it’ll all be going into making this work. This is going to happen.’
Fingers and toes are crossed, Charlotte.
Thanks to New House Country Hotel, Cardiff.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/12.title: Hoping to see your child get into Oxford or Cambridge? A state school may be a better bet than Eton
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/12.subtitle: Use our interactive graphics to discover how many Oxbridge offers pupils at every school in the UK and abroad have received
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/12.text:
Oxford and Cambridge are increasingly shunning pupils from Eton College in favour of children from state schools, new data reveal.
Some of the country’s most prestigious private schools are now seeing their Oxbridge offers decline sharply, according to figures obtained by The Telegraph.
Meanwhile, some state schools have seen their offers soar in recent years and are now among the most successful schools at sending pupils to Oxbridge.
This newspaper has analysed data from both Oxford and Cambridge universities which show the number of offers they have made to every school over the past five years.
Using our interactive graphic, you can now see how many Oxbridge offers pupils at every school in the UK - as well as international schools - have received each year between 2016 and 2020.
Click on each school to examine its Oxbridge success rate, which is calculated by working out how many of its pupils’ applications resulted in offers each year. You can also use the search function to look up a particular school and see how they have fared.
Eton College is one of just three schools which has seen a decline in Oxbridge offers every year since 2016, as top universities come under mounting pressure to accept more students from disadvantaged backgrounds.
The £44,00-a-year boarding school in Windsor has seen its Oxbridge offers plummet by 21 per cent in five years, from 86 in 2016 to 68 in 2020.
Eton's offers are falling even when accounting for the fact fewer of its pupils are now applying to Oxbridge compared to five years ago. The school's success rate - calculated by looking at the proportion of applications which result in offers - has declined by 4.9 percentage points over the same period.
The ten schools that have seen the biggest decline in offers in the past five years are all fee-paying institutions, our data show.
These include Harrow School, the boys’ boarding school, which charges £43,665 per year in fees. It has seen its Oxbridge offers decline by 50 per cent, from 28 to 14.
And Cheltenham Ladies College, a £39,780-a-year girls’ boarding school, has also had a 50 per cent decline in offers, from 26 to 13.
Meanwhile, of the 10 schools which have seen the biggest boost in their Oxbridge offers, all but one are state schools, the majority of which are selective sixth form colleges based in London.
Three schools in the east London borough of Newham - Brampton Manor Academy, London Academy of Excellence and Newham Collegiate Sixth Form - have all seen their offers at least triple over the past five years.
King’s College London Mathematics School and Greenhead College in Huddersfield have both doubled their offers over the same period.
You can use our geographical search tool to find out the best schools are in your local area for getting pupils into Oxbridge.
Simply type in your postcode, and you will get a list of the top 20 schools for Oxbridge offers within a 10-mile radius.
One Oxford don said there has been a “constant drip, drip, drip” of pressure to “move the dial” away from private schools and in favour of state school admissions.
“The dial hadn’t moved basically for 15 years, there was a lot of talk but not much action,” he said. “But now it is happening, even if it’s just at the margin each year. The message has got through. No one likes to be ordered to do anything but after a while it seeps into the consciousness.
“There is also the element that once they have tried and tested the output of Brampton Manor Academy, they think it works, they are good kids, it makes them more confident the next year.”
The Oxford don, who is involved in admissions, said this data would make parents think twice about sending their child to a private school.
“This is a success story - unless you are paying a fortune for your children’s education,” he said. “I think the message is pretty obvious - if you are a family that is set on Oxford or Cambridge, it is a no brainer. You send them to a state sixth form college, you stop paying the high fees and they have the right flag by their name when they apply.”
Barnaby Lenon, chairman of the Independent Schools Council, said that fee-paying institutions remain satisfied that “most of their best applicants” are still getting into Oxbridge and that privately educated pupils are still overrepresented at both universities.
He also pointed out that independent schools are increasingly looking to Ivy League institutions in America - such as Harvard - as destinations for their pupils.
“They are doing this because these are very much the best universities in the world for certain courses and because they offer generous scholarships and bursaries to the best students in the UK,” he said.
Mr Lenon, a former headmaster at Harrow School, also pointed out that some of the top state schools for getting pupils into Oxbridge were originally created by private schools.
“It is important to understand that some of these schools were set up by independent schools in order to help improve the exam results of sixth formers in disadvantaged areas,” he said. “No one has done more to promote these kinds of schools than Eton.”
The London Academy of Excellence, which has more than quadrupled its offers over five years, was set up by a coalition of private schools - including Eton and Harrow - led by Brighton College.
And Harris Westminster Sixth Form - which was set up by the fee-paying Westminster School - has also seen its Oxbridge offers increase fourfold from 10 to 44.
Mr Lenon, who was the first chairman of governors at the London Academy of Excellence, said that the high number of Oxbridge offers that go to pupils from top state schools is “to be welcomed and is not a surprise”.
He explained: “In the last 10 years, these very successful state schools have emerged. And the thing to bear in mind is that they are extremely selective at age 16, to be admitted you need stellar GCSE grades.”
Eton College declined to comment. Oxford and Cambridge both said they have fair and robust admissions policies where they consider all applicants individually and on merit, regardless of which school they attend or what their background is.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/global-healt.title: ‘Carnage’: 375 dead and 630,000 displaced after Typhoon Rai rips through Philippines
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/global-healt.subtitle: Deadly typhoon is the strongest the archipelago has faced this year, with peak winds reaching 146mph
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/global-healt.text:
At least 375 people have been killed after a typhoon tore through the Philippines, causing “complete carnage” and leaving over 630,000 seeking shelter in schools, churches and camps ahead of Christmas.
Typhoon Rai, which hit the country last week, is the strongest the archipelago has faced this year, with peak winds reaching 146mph.
It has left chaos in its wake, with roughly 2.2 million people directly affected – meaning livelihoods and homes have been destroyed, family members lost and health access curtailed. The numbers known to be dead or injured are increasing, according to the Red Cross.
“The fury of this typhoon is something we have not seen for years,” Alberto Bocanegra, the head of delegation of the Philippines Red Cross, told The Telegraph, adding that some areas will not see a return to relative normality for more than a year.
The typhoon struck as the country was finding its feet after the coronavirus pandemic. The Philippines had been one of the hardest hit by the virus in the Asia-Pacific region, recording over 2.8 million cases and more than 50,000 deaths.
But in recent months, vaccinations had ramped up – with 51 per cent of the population receiving one jab – and Covid-19 cases were decreasing.
Mr Bocanegra said officials were concerned that the destruction of services and infrastructure could see cases spike once more. In the past few days, the country saw its first reported cases of the omicron variant.
Mr Bocanegra also expressed the frustration felt by millions across the majority Catholic country who had been gearing up to celebrate Christmas together. “There's great sadness, a great frustration,” he said.
Emergency teams are reporting “complete carnage” in the coastal areas, as homes, hospitals, schools and community buildings have been “ripped to shreds”.
Communication lines remain down, hampering relief efforts and meaning many families are unsure about whether loved ones have survived. Some regions are inaccessible due to landslides and mudslides.
Nine different islands, separated by a distance of more than 800km, sustained ferocious winds and floods, which first hit the country’s southeast coast on Thursday.
At least 375 people have died, making it the deadliest tropical cyclone in 2021. According to the United Nations, 630,000 people are now displaced, while in some areas the roofs of 95 per cent of homes have been ripped off.
“Food supply is running low. Maybe, in a few days, we will totally run out,” said Fely Pedrablanca, the mayor of Tubajon town on Dinagat Island. She added that only nine out of more than 2,000 homes in her town are standing.
Over 200 areas have suffered power outages – and only nine per cent have been restored. It is estimated that some cities may be without electricity for up to three months. Banking systems are also down, meaning locals are struggling to access cash.
A pre-emptive evacuation saw 376,000 people moved to stronger buildings before the first winds hit. But, as the Philippines is an island nation, it is “risky” to move people further afield to safety – for example to other islands by boat – said Dr Liz Stephens, professor of meteorology at the University of Reading.
Dr Stephens said that while the typhoon was predicted a week in advance, the intensity of the storm was not.
“The storm underwent rapid intensification – increasing by 30mph in 24 hours. This is very difficult to predict, and we can’t provide warnings to people in time so they can get out of harm's way,” Dr Stephens said.
Rapid intensification is a “great and increasing cause for concern,” occurring more frequently in recent years, Dr Stephens added.
“Climate change will continue to make storms more intense in the future. Warmer seas means more energy is created,” Dr Stephens said. “And we’re starting to see that already.”
This year tropical cyclones have formed in six major bodies of water. Hurricane Ida, which hit Louisiana in the United States in the autumn, is estimated to have caused $65 billion in damage.
Meanwhile, on Tuesday, the Malaysian military was deployed to distribute food to desperate people trapped in their homes after massive floods hit, leaving over 70,000 displaced.
Days of torrential rain triggered some of the worst flooding in years across the country, swamping cities and villages and cutting off major roads.
Some parts of state capital Shah Alam were still under water Tuesday, and military personnel in boats distributed food to people stuck in their homes and government shelters.
